title: The lonely
hookLine: loneliness is one of today's great poverties
tomorrow: can you disagree with someone and still respect them?

cards: Open your recent calls and scroll past the last week, to names that used to be there and aren't anymore. Somewhere in that list is someone sitting alone tonight with a phone that doesn't ring.

So who is lonely, just one call away from you? An old psalm already knew loneliness is a kind of poverty. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Look thou upon me, and have mercy on me; for I am alone and poor."

teach.b: Here's the question: what does the lonely person need? The tradition's answer starts in the first pages of Genesis.
Adam has a whole garden full of creatures and names every one of them, and God still says: "It is not good for man to be alone." Company isn't a luxury. It's how people were made.
Jesus makes the answer concrete in Matthew.

teach.h: I WAS SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.
teach.b: On the last day the King says, I was sick, and you visited me, and the people ask, when? Whatever you did for the least of these, he answers, you did for me.
So Catholics read a visit to someone alone as a visit to Christ. Now a neighbor tradition, in its own words.
In Islam, a hadith in the collection of Imam Muslim tells of God speaking on the Day of Resurrection: son of Adam, I was sick, and you did not visit me.
The person asks, how could I visit you, when you are the Lord of the worlds? And God answers: didn't you know my servant was sick, and you did not visit him?

teach.h: YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.
teach.b: Had you visited him, you would have found me with him.
What's shared is striking: in both, God meets you at the bedside of the one left alone.
And the honest difference: in Matthew, Christ says you did it to me; Catholics see Christ present in the person.

In the hadith, God says you would have found me with him; Muslims hold that God is never one with any creature, but near. Two ways of saying where God is, ranking neither, and both send you to the same door.

how: Catholics count visiting the sick among the corporal works of mercy, and parishes bring Communion and company to people who can't leave home; in Islam, hadith count visiting the sick among the rights one Muslim has over another.

o: people left alone, in a poverty the psalm names
people who live far from their families
people who prefer to spend their time alone

games.q: alone, and visited — tap the pairs.
p: not good for man to be alone
I was sick, and you visited me
you would have found me with him

s: the psalm puts alone and poor side by side
in the hadith, God says the sick person is God
God says you would have found me with him: near, not the same.
only people who live alone can be lonely
in Genesis, Adam had a whole garden of creatures and was still alone.

games.q: an older coworker eats lunch alone every day and says she's "totally fine." going by the psalm and Matthew 25, what's the move?
o: take her at her word and leave her be.
invite her once, and keep inviting.
mention to a manager that she seems isolated.
games.why: the psalm treats being alone as a need someone can answer, and Matthew 25 counts the visit as done for Christ. one invitation, kept up, is a visit.

practice: Scroll your contacts slowly, and stop at one name: someone who might be alone more than they'd say. Rest your thumb near it and breathe for a while.
Then decide when you'll call, today or tomorrow, and what your first question will be.

wordCard.voice: The lonely. People left alone, in a poverty the psalm already named, often just one call away. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, Genesis 2:18: it is not good for the man to be alone.

carryVoice: Keep this one: a call away, and God at the bedside in both stories. Until tomorrow.
